A positive 1-in-3-SAT instance asks for a truth assignment in which every

no clause contains two chosen variables; covering every element means every
clause contains a chosen variable.  Together: every clause contains exactly
one chosen variable.  Declaring a variable true exactly when its set is
chosen therefore gives a satisfying assignment, and every satisfying
assignment yields such an exact cover.  Variables that occur in no clause

that their truth value is unconstrained.

    universe_size = len(clauses)

    # S[v] = elements of the clauses that contain variable v.
    sets = []
    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        sets.append([c for c, clause in enumerate(clauses) if v in clause])

    return {"universe_size": universe_size, "sets": sets}

Duplicate clauses get distinct universe elements, which is harmless because

"""Polynomial-time reduction from 1-in-3-SAT to Exact Cover.

Idea
----
A positive 1-in-3-SAT instance asks for a truth assignment in which every
clause has *exactly one* true variable.  Build one universe element per
clause and, for every variable v, one set S_v containing the elements of
all clauses in which v occurs.

Choosing a collection of these sets is an exact cover iff the chosen sets
are pairwise disjoint and cover every clause element.  Disjointness means
no clause contains two chosen variables; covering every element means every
clause contains a chosen variable.  Together: every clause contains exactly
one chosen variable.  Declaring a variable true exactly when its set is
chosen therefore gives a satisfying assignment, and every satisfying
assignment yields such an exact cover.  Variables that occur in no clause
give empty sets, which are irrelevant to exact cover, matching the fact
that their truth value is unconstrained.

The construction is linear in the size of the formula.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    clauses = instance["clauses"]
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]

    # One universe element per clause (duplicate clauses get distinct
    # elements, which is harmless: they impose the same constraint).
    universe_size = len(clauses)

    # S[v] = elements of the clauses that contain variable v.
    sets = []
    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        sets.append([c for c, clause in enumerate(clauses) if v in clause])

    return {"universe_size": universe_size, "sets": sets}
